    Getting started with sandtablR

    Raban Heller, Gerhard Achatz

    Source: vignettes/sandtablR.Rmd
    sandtablR.Rmd
    library(sandtablR)

    sandtablR is a framework for mass-casualty incident tabletop exercises: generate a casualty cohort, run it across a board, capture the decisions that were made, then model and explain them.

    The steps below are the whole workflow. Everything the Shiny workbench does, it does by calling these functions.

    1. A cohort

    A cohort is a validated tibble subclass. Every casualty carries a card: demographics, life points, whether they are ventilated, the injury region, and the true sighting category and therapy concept.

    co <- sdt_synthetic_cohort(n = 40, seed = 1)
co
#> # A cohort: 40 casualties
#> # Triage:   red: 18 yellow: 10 green: 12
#>    id      age sex   life_points ventilated injury_region triage therapy
#>    <chr> <int> <chr>       <int> <lgl>      <chr>         <chr>  <chr>  
#>  1 P001     78 m               2 TRUE       multiple      red    TASC   
#>  2 P002     41 m               2 TRUE       thorax        red    DCS    
#>  3 P003     52 m               5 FALSE      extremity     green  none   
#>  4 P004     42 m               4 FALSE      thorax        yellow TASC   
#>  5 P005     31 m               2 TRUE       multiple      red    DCS    
#>  6 P006     45 m               4 FALSE      multiple      yellow TASC   
#>  7 P007     15 f               4 FALSE      extremity     yellow DCS    
#>  8 P008     64 m               6 FALSE      extremity     green  none   
#>  9 P009     44 m               5 FALSE      head          green  none   
#> 10 P010     75 f               1 FALSE      thorax        red    TASC   
#> # ℹ 30 more rows
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: arrival_order <int>

    Marginals come from sdt_reference(), which separates two things that are easy to conflate: values attributed to the published evaluation, and modelling choices sandtablR made where the source does not pin one.

    sdt_reference("published")$triage_mix
#>    red yellow  green 
#>  0.444  0.236  0.319

    Validation is vectorised over columns rather than looping over rows, so a bad import reports everything wrong with it at once rather than one problem per attempt:

    bad <- co
bad$triage <- as.character(bad$triage)
bad$triage[c(2, 5)] <- "purple"
bad$life_points[3] <- 99
sdt_cohort(bad)
#> Error in `sdt_cohort()`:
#> ! `x` is not a valid cohort.
#> ✖ triage: must be one of "red", "yellow", and "green" in row 2 and 5.
#> ✖ life_points: must lie in 0:6 in row 3.

    2. A scenario

    A scenario is a cohort plus the board’s resource capacities.

    sc <- sdt_scenario(co, resources = list(or = 3, icu_imc = 6, ward = 20),
                   name = "concert")
sc
#> <scenario> concert: 40 casualties
#> triage mix — red: 18, yellow: 10, green: 12
#> resources — triage: 1, ed_red: 1, ed_yellow: 1, diagnostics: 1, or: 3, recovery: 1, icu_imc: 6, ward: 20, green_area: 1, morgue: 1, external: 1, not_seen: 1
summary(sc)
#> # A cohort: 8 casualties
#> # Triage:   red: 2 yellow: 3 green: 3
#>   triage therapy     n
#>   <chr>  <chr>   <int>
#> 1 green  DCS         1
#> 2 green  TASC        2
#> 3 green  none        9
#> 4 red    DCS         5
#> 5 red    TASC       13
#> 6 yellow DCS         4
#> 7 yellow TASC        5
#> 8 yellow none        1
    sdt_plot_triage_mix(sc)

    Bar chart of casualties per sighting category. Synthetic demonstration.

    3. Simulate patient flow

    sdt_simulate() maps the scenario onto a discrete-event model and routes each casualty by sighting category and therapy concept.

    run <- sdt_simulate(sc, replications = 5, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
run
#> <game_run> 5 replications over 270 minutes
#> 42 casualty records, 455 area events

    The engine’s real output is the event log: one row per casualty per board area, with when it entered and left.

    head(run$events)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   replication id     step area         start    end duration service_time
#>         <int> <chr> <int> <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1           1 P001      1 triage        1.86  10.00     8.14         8.14
#> 2           1 P001      2 ed_red       10.00  21.3     11.3         11.3 
#> 3           1 P001      3 diagnostics  21.3   40.0     18.7         18.7 
#> 4           1 P001      4 or           40.0  103.      62.9         62.9 
#> 5           1 P001      5 icu_imc     103.   153.      49.8         49.8 
#> 6           1 P002      1 triage        6.07  21.3     15.2          3.73

    Three dispositions are terminal by design, and that is what reproduces the published end-of-game distribution: critical care is where a casualty stays, a ward bed is the end of the line, and a casualty who is worked up but not taken to theatre is still being held in the emergency department when the game is called.

    The quickest way to see what the engine did is to look at the board. Every casualty is a point in the area it had reached at that moment, laid out as the nine areas of the published board. Change at and you watch the stream move across it.

    sdt_plot_board(run, at = 150)

    The nine board areas with casualties drawn as coloured points. Synthetic demonstration. 

    summary(run, reference = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 6
#>   area        label                    n proportion reference difference
#>   <chr>       <chr>                <int>      <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 triage      Screening              109      0.545      0.08      0.465
#> 2 ed          Emergency department    23      0.115      0.16     -0.045
#> 3 diagnostics Radiology                3      0.015      0.04     -0.025
#> 4 or          Operating room           7      0.035      0.11     -0.075
#> 5 recovery    Recovery                 0      0          0.01     -0.01 
#> 6 icu_imc     ICU / IMC               28      0.14       0.23     -0.09 
#> 7 ward        Ward                    30      0.15       0.35     -0.2  
#> 8 not_seen    Not yet seen             0      0          0         0
    sdt_plot_end_state(run)

    Simulated end-of-game location against the published reference. Synthetic demonstration.

    That calibration is checkable rather than asserted: sdt_reference_scenario() builds the board the engine was tuned on, and the package’s own test suite re-runs the comparison.

    4. Decision paths

    Because the event log records every area entry, each casualty has a full ordered pathway.

    head(sdt_decision_paths(run), 8)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 7
#>   replication id     step area         start    end duration
#>         <int> <chr> <int> <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1           1 P001      1 triage        1.86  10.00     8.14
#> 2           1 P001      2 ed_red       10.00  21.3     11.3 
#> 3           1 P001      3 diagnostics  21.3   40.0     18.7 
#> 4           1 P001      4 or           40.0  103.      62.9 
#> 5           1 P001      5 icu_imc     103.   153.      49.8 
#> 6           1 P002      1 triage        6.07  21.3     15.2 
#> 7           1 P002      2 ed_red       21.3   40.0     18.7 
#> 8           1 P002      3 diagnostics  40.0   46.1      6.11

    sdt_decision_consistency() asks how repeatably the same casualty was handled across replications, as a distance between its pathways rather than agreement on a single label.

    consistency <- sdt_decision_consistency(run)
head(consistency[order(consistency$consistency), ])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   id    n_paths n_distinct consistency
#>   <chr>   <int>      <int>       <dbl>
#> 1 P019        5          3       0.44 
#> 2 P014        5          3       0.45 
#> 3 P020        5          3       0.5  
#> 4 P022        5          4       0.508
#> 5 P021        5          3       0.517
#> 6 P010        5          4       0.525
    sdt_plot_sequences(run, type = "distribution")

    Share of casualties in each board area by position in the pathway. Synthetic demonstration.

    With TraMineR and WeightedCluster installed, sdt_seq_cluster() groups pathways into a few characteristic routes through the board.

    5. Model the decisions

    The card’s true category follows from life points by construction, so every engine scores near 1 on it and the comparison says nothing. What is worth modelling is what a participant called. sdt_add_decisions() simulates that using the published per-category hit rates.

    labelled <- sdt_add_decisions(co, seed = 2)
sdt_consistency_score(labelled$triage, labelled$called_triage)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate     n
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl> <int>
#> 1 kap     multiclass     0.563    40
    fit <- sdt_fit(labelled, target = "called_triage", engine = "tree",
               tune = FALSE, folds = 3, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
fit
#> <sdt_model> tree (glass-box) -> called_triage, roc_auc 0.606
#> 5 predictors: age, sex, life_points, ventilated, injury_region
sdt_metrics(fit)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   .metric  .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>    <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 accuracy multiclass     0.583
#> 2 f_meas   macro          0.5  
#> 3 kap      multiclass     0.333
#> 4 roc_auc  hand_till      0.606

    sdt_workflowset() screens every installed engine onto one leaderboard, with glass-box and black-box models side by side. See vignette("model-bench", package = "sandtablR").

    6. Explain

    Explanations are model-agnostic, so the same views work on a decision tree and on a random forest.

    sdt_importance(fit, n_permutations = 5)

    Permutation variable importance. Synthetic demonstration.

    The workbench

    sdt_run_app() launches an interactive workbench over all of the above: build a scenario, run the board, annotate decisions, train and compare models, explain them, and analyse decision paths. It also renders the session to a self-contained HTML report.

    Provenance

    The domain model (sighting categories, ETC/DCS/TASC therapy concepts, board areas, patient-card fields) follows the TDSC tabletop exercise as described in the open-access evaluation by Achatz et al. (2023), Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg 49(2):607–617, doi:10.1007/s00068-022-02217-1. sandtablR is a generic re-implementation built from published specifications, and is not affiliated with the TDSC course.

    Save and reproduce a run 

    path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(list(scenario = sc, run = run, seed = 1,
             session = sessionInfo()), path)
restored <- readRDS(path)
stopifnot(identical(run$events, restored$run$events))

    Retain the software revision and scenario alongside every seed. A reproducible simulation is not evidence that its assumptions describe a real incident. See the model bench for a separate synthetic prediction example.
